item.title: “Form, monks, is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of form — that too is impermanent. Form that has arisen from the impermanent,…
item.description:
“Form, monks, is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of form — that too is impermanent. Form that has arisen from the impermanent, monks, how could it be permanent? Feeling, monks, is impermanent … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of consciousness — that too is impermanent. Consciousness that has arisen from the impermanent, monks, how could it be permanent? Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … disenchanted with feeling … disenchanted with perception … disenchanted with formations … disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate … He knows: ‘… there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.18

item.title: “Cunda, I do not teach merely for the sake of preventing defilements in the present life. Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma only for…
item.description:
“Cunda, I do not teach merely for the sake of preventing defilements in the present life. Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma only for the sake of eradicating defilements in the future. Cunda, I teach the Dhamma both for preventing defilements in the present life and for eradicating defilements in the future.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 29 – Pāsādikasutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these five defilements of the mind because of which the mind becomes defiled, not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these five defilements of the mind because of which the mind becomes defiled, not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not properly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements. What five? Sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt. These five defilements of the mind, monks, because of which the mind becomes defiled, not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not properly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.23

item.title: Elder Nun Abhirūpa Nandā: Nandā, look at this body — A collection of many diseases, impure, Full of stench, rotting. Develop your mind, Contemplate the…
item.description:
Elder Nun Abhirūpa Nandā:

Nandā, look at this body —
A collection of many diseases, impure,
Full of stench, rotting.
Develop your mind,
Contemplate the nature of foulness,
Achieve one-pointedness,
With mind well concentrated.

Practice the signless,
Abandon the underlying tendency to conceit.
By fully understanding conceit,
You will live at peace.

From: Therīgāthā 2.1

item.title: “And how, monks, is a monk called a ‘noble one’? He has made distant evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful,…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is a monk called a ‘noble one’? He has made distant evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful, producing painful results, leading to future birth, aging, and death. Thus, monks, a monk is called a noble one.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 39 – Mahāhatthipadopamasutta

item.title: “Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye and saw beings with little dust in their…
item.description:
“Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye and saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with sharp faculties and with dull faculties, with good dispositions and with bad dispositions, some easy to teach and some hard to teach, and a few who saw the danger in rebirth in another world and the danger of faulty actions. Just as in a blue lotus pond, a red lotus pond, or a white lotus pond, some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, do not rise above the water, and are nourished underwater; some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and reach the water’s surface; some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, rise up above the water and are not wetted by the water.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 14 – Mahāpadānasutta

item.title: - “Venerable sir, I do not understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One regarding the purpose of purity of virtue.” - “Monk, if you…
item.description:
- “Venerable sir, I do not understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One regarding the purpose of purity of virtue.” - “Monk, if you do not understand the Dhamma I have taught regarding the purpose of purity of virtue, then how, monk, do you understand the Dhamma I have taught?” - “Venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One as greed and the removal of greed.” - “Good, good, monk! Good, monk! You understand the Dhamma taught by me as greed and the removal of greed. It is for the purpose of greed and the removal of greed, monk, that the Dhamma is taught by me. What do you think, monk: Is the eye permanent or impermanent?” - “Impermanent, venerable sir.” - “The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … Is the mind permanent or impermanent?” - “Impermanent, venerable sir.” - “What is impermanent — is that suffering or happiness?” - “Suffering, venerable sir.” - “What is impermanent, suffering, subject to change — is it fitting to regard it as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” - “No, venerable sir.” - “Seeing thus, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye … disenchanted with the mind … Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate … He knows: ‘… there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.74

item.title: The hunter set his trap and snare, The wise deer does not approach, Having eaten the crops, we go our way, Leaving the trapper to…
item.description:
The hunter set his trap and snare,
The wise deer does not approach,
Having eaten the crops, we go our way,
Leaving the trapper to lament.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 82 – Raṭṭhapālasutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these three things. What three? Sensual thought, ill-will thought, harmful thought. Monks, these are the three things. To abandon these three things,…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these three things. What three? Sensual thought, ill-will thought, harmful thought. Monks, these are the three things. To abandon these three things, three things should be developed. What three? To abandon sensual thought, the thought of renunciation should be developed. To abandon ill-will thought, the thought of non-ill-will should be developed. To abandon harmful thought, the thought of harmlessness should be developed. To abandon those three things, monks, these three things should be developed.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.109

item.title: “Suppose, Rādha, young boys or girls are playing with sandcastles. As long as their desire, lust, love, thirst, passion, and craving for those sandcastles are…
item.description:
“Suppose, Rādha, young boys or girls are playing with sandcastles. As long as their desire, lust, love, thirst, passion, and craving for those sandcastles are not fully abandoned, they still cling to them, delight in them, treasure them, and are attached to them. But when their desire, lust, love, thirst, passion, and craving for those sandcastles are fully abandoned, then they smash them, scatter them, demolish them with their hands and feet and no longer play with them. So too, Rādha, you should smash, scatter, demolish form and not play with it, being intent on the destruction of craving for form. The destruction of craving, Rādha, is Nibbāna.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.2
